item.title: In Utero MRI of Radial Glial Fibers Highlights Their Role in Modulating Fetal Cortical Folding
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The process of cortical folding is fundamental to early human brain development. While the differential growth of the cortical layers is a known driver, the biomechanical contribution of key cellular microstructures remains unclear, and there is a lack of direct in vivo markers of cortical microstructures for time-resolved observations. Using a multimodal approach combining in utero and ex vivo fetal brain MRI, histology, and computational mechanical simulation, we investigated whether developmental reorganization of cortical radial microstructures, particularly the radial glial cell (RGC)-associated scaffold, is linked to cortical folding and may modulate its mechanical progression. We characterized this radial organization noninvasively using diffusion MRI-based radial fiber density ( FD rad ). ex vivo fetal brain MRI and histology supported that regional variations in FD rad were strongly associated with vimentin-labelled radial architecture. Our in utero MRI data revealed closely coordinated developmental changes in cortical FD rad and curvature, with their regional timings and spatial patterns significantly coupled across the cortex. Longitudinal in utero MRI data further supported the synchronized within-individual co-development of FD rad and curvature. Furthermore, biomechanical simulations showed that reducing radial reinforcement modulated differential-growth-driven buckling, producing earlier folding and a greater cortical curvature under otherwise matched model conditions. Collectively, this study introduces FD rad as a noninvasive in utero MRI measure sensitive to radial glial fibers. By integrating spatial, temporal, histological, and computational evidence, our findings suggested a model in which developmental disassembly of the radial scaffold may modulate the mechanical response of the fetal cortex to differential growth, thereby contributing to cortical folding.

item.title: The Aging Brain Matrix: Cross-Species Evidence Linking FREM3 to Brain and Cognitive Aging
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The human extracellular-matrix-related FREM3 gene is strongly age-dependent, enriched in age-sensitive excitatory long-range-projecting neurons, and implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. To establish the first translationally relevant causal evidence for the gene’s roles in brain structure and cognition, we developed an excitatory-neuron-specific Frem3 conditional knockout mouse model ( Frem3 -cKO) and computed genetically regulated expression of FREM3 ( FREM3 -GReX) in humans, enabling convergent neurostructural and cognitive characterizations. Frem3 -cKO mice showed widespread lower global and regional brain volume in middle age vs young adulthood, consistent with drastic age-dependent volume loss absent in wildtype mice. These effects were strongest in cognitively relevant cortical regions and paralleled by lower cognitive performance. In humans, lower FREM3- GReX was associated with lower total surface area, which further mediated an indirect link to lower cognitive performance across multiple age-sensitive domains. We provide the first translationally relevant cross-species evidence supporting a key role for FREM3/Frem3 in maintaining brain and cognitive health across aging.

item.title: A Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman Kernel Framework for Multimodal Brain Connectome Analysis
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract We introduce a Wasserstein Weisfeiler-Lehman (WWL) graph-kernel framework for the joint analysis of weighted structural graphs and continuous node attributes, together with a regularized fractional-Laplacian extension of the underlying graph propagation operator. The proposed fractional operator provides non-local propagation across the entire graph, with influence decaying as a power law with graph distance, while remaining anchored to the subject-specific structural topology. This extends the standard finite-range Weisfeiler Lehman propagation scheme to a controlled long-range setting without introducing an externally prescribed coupling between structural and functional information. We formulate the framework for multimodal brain connectivity by representing each subject as a single attributed graph: diffusion tractography defines the weighted structural edges, while resting-state functional connectivity profiles are encoded as continuous node attributes. We evaluate the method on a synthetic cohort of $900$ subjects in three ordered clinical groups along the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, generated from multiple structural templates and characterised by a spatially structured loss of resting-state network segregation with age. Under nested cross-validation, the WWL kernel achieves a balanced accuracy of $0.651\pm0.028$, significantly outperforming both a raw-feature SVM and a histogram-based WL-kernel baseline. Controlled ablations separate the contribution of the Wasserstein representation from that of structural propagation. Replacing the propagation operator by the identity yields essentially identical classification performance, whereas a structure-only representation approaches chance, showing that the discriminative gain in this benchmark is primarily associated with the Wasserstein point-cloud representation rather than structural propagation. Conversely, experiments across distinct signal regimes show that the fractional extension is signal-dependent: non-local propagation can improve continuous prediction for diffuse whole-brain coupling signals, but provides no consistent advantage for network-segregation signals. We further identify a connectivity artefact induced by fixed-percentile structural sparsification and establish a threshold preserving graph connectivity across subjects. The results clarify the respective roles of Wasserstein geometry, structural propagation, and non-locality in multimodal graph representations and provide a controlled framework for assessing when fractional graph propagation is expected to be beneficial.

item.title: Cerebellar subregions support social cognition in early behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Social cognitive deficits manifest early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD), compromising individuals' ability to interpret social cues, empathize, and maintain interpersonal relationships. Current neurobiological models emphasize cortical network disruption, particularly within the salience, semantic appraisal, and default mode networks, as primary contributors to social dysfunction. However, despite the increasingly recognized role of the cerebellum in higher-order cognitive and socioemotional processes, its contributions to social deficits remains underexplored in bvFTD. Here, we investigated the unique and network-level influences of cerebellar subregions on social cognition across experimental and real-world assessments in early-stage bvFTD. A total of 107 individuals with bvFTD and 100 healthy controls were evaluated across three social domains: theory of mind (ToM) (The Awareness of Social Inference Test-Social Inference-Enriched, TASIT-SIE; Cognitive Emotional Perspective Taking Test), emotion reading (Dynamic Affect Recognition Test; TASIT-Emotion Evaluation Test; Comprehensive Affect Testing System), and real-life empathy (Revised Self-Monitoring Scale; Interpersonal Reactivity Index). Using a functional cerebellar parcellation, we extracted volumes of posterior cerebellar subregions implicated in social-linguistic and multiple-demand networks from participants' structural MRIs. To address the high collinearity between cerebellar and cortical atrophy patterns, we applied sequential regression, partial least squares correlation, and dominance analysis to characterize brain-behavior relationships. Additionally, supplementary structural equation modelling (SEM) examined whether the associations between cerebellar integrity and social cognition was mediated by executive functioning. Our results showed that cerebellar subregional integrity contributed to social cognitive deficits in individuals with early-stage bvFTD. Cerebellar subregions, particularly right Crus I and II, showed the strongest and most selective contribution to high-level inferential Theory of Mind performance. Tasks involving dynamic emotion stimuli exhibited a more distributed pattern of cerebello-cerebral involvement. By contrast, questionnaire-based measures of real-world social functioning were less prominently represented in the latent covariance structure. SEM further showed that cerebellar integrity remained directly associated with social cognition after accounting for executive functioning, whereas the indirect association through executive functioning was not significant. These findings highlight the task-dependent nature of cerebellar involvement in social cognition, and demonstrate that time-limited experimental tasks, particularly those involving inferential reasoning about beliefs and affect, are likely to be especially valuable in detecting subtle cerebello-cerebral network dysfunction that questionnaire-based measures may overlook. Our results extend cortex-centric models of social dysfunction in bvFTD by demonstrating that cerebellar subregions contribute to distributed cerebello-cerebral systems associated with social cognitive performance. These findings provide a foundation for future longitudinal and mechanistic studies of cerebello-cerebral dysfunction in neurodegenerative disease.

item.title: Cross-metric convergence reveals altered white matter microstructural-functional correspondence in bipolar ii disorder.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
White matter (WM) microstructural abnormalities are increasingly recognized in bipolar II disorder (BD-II), but it remains unclear how tract-wise microstructural organization corresponds to WM functional connectivity. Diffusion MRI and resting-state fMRI data were acquired from 86 patients with BD-II and 84 healthy controls (HCs). Microstructural profile similarity (MPS) and functional connectivity (FC) matrices were constructed across 48 WM tracts. Following participant-wise, modality-specific standardization of the MPS and FC matrices, tract-wise correspondence was quantified using Spearman correlation and Euclidean profile distance, with self-connections excluded. Group differences were assessed using covariate-adjusted linear models with false discovery rate correction. Sensitivity analyses assessed robustness to clinical sample restrictions and methodological choices. BD-II showed altered MPS-FC correspondence in a restricted set of WM tracts, with 4 tracts identified by Spearman correlation and 6 by Euclidean distance. The left posterior corona radiata (PCR_L) and left external capsule (EC_L) showed convergent abnormalities across both metrics, characterized by higher rank-order correspondence and lower profile distance in BD-II. These convergent findings were stable across several sensitivity analyses but were sensitive to the diffusion-feature normalization reference and Euclidean profile scaling. Neither tract was significantly associated with symptom severity after multiple-comparison correction, whereas exploratory analyses implicated the left uncinate fasciculus in depressive symptom variation. BD-II is associated with altered correspondence between WM microstructural and functional organization. These findings provide multimodal evidence for atypical WM organization and extend current understanding of the neurobiological alterations associated with BD-II.

item.title: Prefrontal circuitry abnormalities and cognitive impairment in adolescents with early-onset psychosis.
item.description:
European child & adolescent psychiatry
Early-onset psychosis (EOP) is associated with marked cognitive impairment and poorer health-related and psychosocial outcomes compared to adult-onset illness, yet the neural mechanisms underlying these deficits during adolescence remain incompletely understood. Despite evidence implicating dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) dysfunction, the region's functional and structural correlates in youth with EOP are not well characterized. Adolescents with EOP (N=31) and healthy controls (HC; N=20) completed NIH Toolbox cognitive assessments and PROMIS self-reports. Prefrontal function was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) during a Stroop task and at rest. Multimodal MRI, including resting-state fMRI, diffusion tensor imaging, and structural imaging, was used to examine connectivity and morphology of prefrontal and fronto-cerebellar circuits. Adolescents with EOP exhibited poorer cognitive performance across executive functioning domains compared to HC. fNIRS revealed reduced right dlPFC activation on a cognitive control paradigm (p=0.007, pfdr=0.04) and a trend of increased resting-state connectivity between right dlPFC and ventrolateral PFC (p=0.02, pfdr=0.9). Furthermore, resting-state fMRI showed increased dlPFC-striatal connectivity with striatal regions and reduced connectivity with cerebellar Crus I/II (p-FDR<0.05). White matter integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus correlated with dlPFC activation during task performance. Structural analyses identified reduced frontal cortical thickness and decreased cerebellar Crus II volumes (p-FWE<0.05) in patients with EOP, with frontal morphology associating with cognitive measures. Cognitive impairment in adolescents with EOP is associated with convergent abnormalities in dlPFC function, fronto-striatal connectivity, and fronto-cerebellar structure. These findings provide preliminary support for a model of disrupted prefrontal circuitry in EOP and highlight the potential clinical value of multimodal imaging markers.

item.title: Claustrum Morphometry Reveals Spatially Heterogeneous Alterations in 22q11DS
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human claustrum is a small, irregular, and complexly positioned structure, yet it carries long range projections to most cortical regions responsible for executive functioning. Prior structural MRI research has largely relied on global volume as the metric of its morphology. Such measures may obscure regionally specific morphological changes relevant to developmental and pathological variation. We therefore addressed this limitation by applying longitudinal surface-based morphometry to 874 scans from 440 individuals aged 5-35 years, comparing typical development with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS), a genetic condition characterized by brain dysmaturation, and assessing associations with working memory performance. Our data show a significant age-related volumetric decline that is reduced in 22q11DS left claustra, while surface deformation and thickness analyses revealed spatial patterns unique to hemisphere, group, and developmental age. In controls, the claustrum surface deformed with age in clustered zones along a dorsoventral gradient, and the dorsal-anterior zone thinned across development while the ventral zone thickened. 22q11DS claustra showed less age-related deformation than controls, whose claustrum surface changes associated with verbal working memory. This structural correlate was statistically equivalent to zero in carriers, consistent with a disrupted claustral development to the working memory vulnerability of the syndrome. These findings show the value of surface‑based morphometry over volume alone, highlight dysmaturation and regionally organized claustrum shape variation, and suggest that disrupted structural organization is accompanied by a weaker claustrum-working memory association.

item.title: Divergence from Diffusion Tensor: a discriminant diffusion marker from single shell MRI
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Purpose: The Divergence from the Diffusion Tensor (DDT) is a new diffusion MRI metric that quantifies how the measured diffusion signal separates from the tensor assumption. It is marker for tissue heterogeneity that is estimated from single-shell data and can be used in brain studies. Methods: There exist other techniques that allow the calculation of how the measured diffusion diverges from the Gaussian and tensor assumptions. However, the calculation requires large data-sets with different b-values, which makes them incompatible which standard diffusion tensor acquisitions. By imposing an initial assumption, an alternative formulation based on one single shell (ie, single b-value) is reported. Results: Publicly available databases are used to test the behavior of DDT against other anisotropy measures. It shows the ability to discriminate different non-Gaussian diffusion scenarios with very low intra-subject variabilities. Conclusions: DDT can extract relevant information from the white matter, without any additional demands on data acquisition and totally compatible with standard diffusion MRI analysis pipelines. This makes DDT a good candidate to be used as an imaging marker for brain studies.

item.title: Impact of Chatbot-Based Cognitive Training on Cognitive Function and White Matter Integrity in Cognitively Unimpaired Older Adults: Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
JMIR aging
Background Cognitive training may enhance cognition and support brain health during aging, but few trials have evaluated readily accessible chatbot-based programs with neuroimaging outcomes. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the effects of a chatbot-based cognitive training program on white matter microstructural organization and cognition in cognitively unimpaired older adults. Methods In a single-blind randomized controlled trial, 72 cognitively unimpaired older adults were assigned to chatbot-based cognitive training (30 min/day, 5 days/week for 12 weeks; n=37) or a no-intervention control (n=35). Diffusion tensor imaging at baseline and 12 weeks quantified fractional anisotropy (FA) in predefined white matter tracts, and cognition was assessed with the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery. Results Groups were comparable at baseline. After 12 weeks, the training group showed significantly less FA reduction than controls in the bilateral tapetum and right posterior thalamic radiation, surviving false discovery rate control (P<.05). The training group also improved on Paired Associates Learning (PAL), an episodic memory measure (P=.04). PAL improvement was positively associated with FA change in the right posterior thalamic radiation and right sagittal stratum (false discovery rate-adjusted P=.04 for each). Conclusions These findings suggest that a 12-week chatbot-based cognitive training program may support episodic memory and the relative maintenance of white matter microstructural organization in selected pathways in cognitively unimpaired older adults, consistent with a brain-maintenance framework. Trial registration CRIS KCT0004630; https://tinyurl.com/4xfesb68.

item.title: Individualized structural brain network and transcriptomic characterization of heterogeneity in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a heterogeneous metabolic disorder that also affects the brain, yet prior neuroimaging studies have predominantly focused on group-level comparisons, obscuring interindividual variability in brain structural organization. To capture this heterogeneity, we constructed individualized differential structural covariance networks for 156 individuals with T2DM using 148 healthy controls as a normative reference. Unsupervised clustering based on these individualized networks revealed two neuroanatomical subtypes with distinct network configurations. Most subtype-differentiating edges showed higher values in one subtype, whereas a smaller set of edges, primarily involving the basal ganglia and cerebellum, showed higher values in the other. Integration with transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas identified genes spatially associated with subtype-related differences. These genes were enriched in processes including receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and glycerolipid metabolism, with preferential expression in the striatum and cerebellum. Together, these findings characterize interindividual variation in brain structural covariance in T2DM and identify candidate molecular processes associated with the observed subtype differences.

item.title: Graph Neural Network Reveals the Cortical Morphology of Local Brain Aging in Normal Cognition and Alzheimer's Disease.
item.description:
Neuroinformatics
Estimating brain age (BA) from T1-weighted magnetic resonance images (MRIs) provides a powerful framework for quantifying anatomical brain aging. Whereas global BA (GBA) summarizes overall brain health, local BA (LBA) provides cortically specific patterns of aging at the subject level. Although previous studies have examined anatomical contributors to GBA, to our knowledge, no framework has been established to estimate LBA using cortical morphology. To address this gap, we introduce a graph neural network (GNN) that uses morphometric features-cortical thickness, surface area, curvature, gray/white matter intensity ratio (GWR), sulcal depth-to estimate LBA across the cortical surface at high spatial resolution (mean inter-vertex distance = 1.37 mm). Trained on cortical surface meshes extracted from the MRIs of cognitively normal (CN) adults (N = 14,423), our model achieves better test-retest performance than the existing state-of-the-art, while identifying more biologically plausible patterns of aging in Alzheimer's disease (AD) on the ADNI dataset. Association cortices emerge as primary sites of morphometric aging in CNs, whereas mild cognitive impairment is characterized by widespread aging that is pronounced in the parahippocampal gyrus. AD subjects demonstrate significant aging across the entire cortex, particularly within medial temporal regions and associated cortical networks. Feature ablation highlights curvature and GWR as preferentially sensitive to AD pathology. Regional LBA gaps are significantly associated with neuropsychological measures of AD-related cognitive impairment, linking cortical aging patterns to clinical outcomes. These results demonstrate that GNN-based modeling of cortical morphometry enables biologically interpretable mapping of local brain aging with greater fidelity than prior work.

item.title: Microstructure of white matter association tracts in the temporal lobe predicts the timing of electrophysiological activity and behaviour in picture naming
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
White matter (WM) microstructure has been mainly associated with accuracy of picture naming. However, little is known about how WM properties relate to the timing of picture naming and its underlying electrophysiological activity. Here, we linked diffusion-weighted, electrophysiological, and behavioural data, using time-based measures to conceptually connect WM deterioration to alterations in conduction speed and precision. Our sample included individuals of varying age, with or without stroke. We correlated fractional anisotropy (FA) of bilateral WM tracts traversing the temporal lobe with mean response times (RTs) and response time variability (coefficient of variation, CV) in picture naming, and with the onset latency of neuronal activity, represented by the electrophysiological P2 component time-locked to picture onset. We selected tracts showing associations with P2 latency and naming performance separately, on which we conducted path analyses examining the relationship between structure, neuronal activity and behaviour. Depending on the tract, higher FA was associated with faster and/or more consistent naming, suggesting that ventral tracts differentially contribute to naming speed and consistency. Importantly, path modelling for the right inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus (IFOF) revealed that FA predicted P2 latency, which in turn predicted RTs, possibly reflecting a structure-activity-behaviour relationship in lexical-semantic processing. P2 source reconstruction demonstrated anatomical proximity to posterior segments of the right IFOF, supporting these findings. Overall, this study provides a proof of concept for modelling structure-activity-behaviour relationships in language research, while highlighting the need for elaboration of such relations at a more mechanistic level.

item.title: Habitual sleep duration is associated with the cortical organisation of brain network controllability
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Sleep is fundamental to adaptive brain function, yet how habitual sleep relates to the structural network properties that support flexible transitions between brain states remains poorly understood. Combining wrist-accelerometer sleep measures with diffusion MRI connectomes from 15,799 UK Biobank adults, we show that longer workday sleep is associated with higher modal controllability of somatomotor systems and lower controllability of visual cortex. This system-specific signature reproduced in a locked test set (n = 4,740) and was robust across extensive sensitivity analyses. Decomposition showed that it reflects a redistribution of structural connection weight, with greater absolute visual connectivity and a smaller somatomotor share of the whole-brain total. Weekend catch-up sleep showed no comparable association. The signature was distinct from brain-ageing patterns and, across 1,226 phenotypes, related mainly to physical activity and body composition rather than cognition. These findings link everyday sleep habits to the system-specific organisation of brain network controllability.

item.title: Insula functional connectivity development follows a canonical antero-posterior axis of organization
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The insula is a heterogeneous region associated with a range of functional domains including sensory, cognitive, and emotional processing. Cytoarchitectural and functional studies have described an antero-posterior axis of insula organization. However, the insula's functional development remains sparsely described. We delineated the development of insula resting-state functional connectivity across 562 individuals (6-22 years) using generalized additive models and population value decomposition. We show insulo-cortical functional connectivity development differs across the insula: anterior subregions have predominantly decreasing connectivity across the age range examined, whereas posterior subregions have variable connectivity that aligns with the sensorimotor-association axis. Vertex-level analysis revealed that age-related trajectories followed an antero-posterior axis that aligned with estimates of insula microstructure. Our results emphasize that the development of insula connectivity is spatially heterogeneous and aligns with known cytoarchitecture. The normative insula development described here provides a foundation for investigating how emerging psychopathology may be linked to variation in insula development.

item.title: Brain Age Gap Associations with Externalising Behaviours in Youth: A Longitudinal Investigation in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Cohort
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Early adolescence is a period of heightened risk for the emergence of externalising psychopathology, making it an important window for identifying neurodevelopmental risk markers. Differences between predicted brain age and chronological age - termed the brain age gap - reflect variation from age-typical patterns of brain structure. While brain age gap has been closely linked with internalising behaviours in adolescence, less is known about its relationship with externalising symptoms. This study examined whether brain age gap in late childhood/early adolescence (9-11 years) is associated with current externalising symptoms and whether it predicts externalising trajectories over seven-year follow-up. Methods. Participants were 10,516 adolescents (aged 9-11 at baseline; up to 18 years at follow-up) from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study who met inclusion/exclusion criteria. Brain age gap for each participant was derived from an external validated prediction model (Drobinin et al., 2022) applied to baseline measurements of cortical volume, area, and subcortical volume. Linear mixed-effects models were used to test cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline brain age gap and externalising symptoms, as assessed using the Child Behaviour Checklist. Primary models were adjusted for age, sex, pubertal status, and prior to inclusion of sociodemographic covariates (ethnoracial identity and caregiver highest education). Results. A higher/more positive brain age gap was associated with greater externalising symptoms at baseline (B[SE]=0.067[0.033], p=.042), but this association was removed following sociodemographic adjustment (B[SE]=0.056[0.033], p=.088). Longitudinally, a significant brain age gap x age interaction was identified that remained evident after sociodemographic adjustment, with this relationship weakening across adolescence (B[SE]=-0.007[0.003], p=.033). Conclusions. These findings suggest that a more positive brain age gap, indicating more mature-appearing brain structure for age, in late childhood/early adolescence may be associated with externalising psychopathology, but this relationship is likely to be age- and context-dependent rather than a stable marker of persistent behavioural risk.

item.title: Neuroimaging Correlates of Adolescent Substance Use: A Systematic Review of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background: Neuroimaging may help characterize brain and contextual factors associated with substance use during development. The ABCD study supports investigation of developmental pathways relevant to substance use [1]. Objective: To synthesize original ABCD publications examining MRI measures in relation to substance use and substance-related exposures. Methods: The authors screened all 2,700 publications in the ABCD corpus. Original empirical articles reporting an MRI measure of any modality and a substance use variable were eligible; methodological, conceptual, review, and commentary articles were excluded. Imaging modality, brain measures, substances, design, and association direction were extracted for descriptive synthesis. Results: The evidence considered spans morphology, white matter microstructure, resting-state connectivity, and task activation. Findings concerning youth initiation, prenatal exposure, and familial liability address distinct developmental questions. Family history and stressful life events feature in the white matter literature [2]. Findings vary by modality, exposure definition, and temporal direction, and include null associations. Conclusions: The literature suggests distributed and context-dependent neuroimaging associations. Observational designs, overlapping participants, confounding, and analytic heterogeneity limit causal interpretation and assessment of independent replication. The findings support further longitudinal investigation but do not establish a validated MRI screening tool.

item.title: Investigating the Association of Physical Activity and Muscular Fitness with Structural Brain Changes and Cognitive Performance
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Physical activity (PA) is a modifiable factor linked to cognitive decline, but its relationship with structural brain changes remains inconsistent. We studied associations of self-reported PA and handgrip strength with brain structure and cognition. Methods We examined middle-aged to elderly participants from the population-based Hamburg City Health Study, who underwent brain MRI and cognitive testing. PA was assessed via questionnaires (overall PA, sport participation, strength training frequency), and handgrip strength indexed muscular fitness. MRI markers included among others peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD), cortical thickness, and structural connectivity metrics. Cognition was assessed with CERAD-Plus subtests. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression and mediation analysis. Results Among 2,618 participants (mean age 64 ± 8.3 years; 44% female), higher handgrip strength was associated with lower PSMD (β=-0.117, 95% CI [-0.194, -0.041]), greater cortical thickness (β = 0.100, 95% CI [0.019, 0.181]), and faster processing speed (β=-0.155, 95% CI [-0.234, -0.076]). Self-reported PA showed no associations with brain structure. Sport participation was associated with faster processing speed (β=-0.059, 95% CI [-0.105, -0.014]), better executive function (β=-0.045, 95% CI [-0.088, -0.002]), and better verbal memory (β = 0.052, 95% CI [0.007, 0.097]). PSMD partially mediated the association between handgrip strength and processing speed (ab=-0.008, 95% CI [-0.019, -0.001]). Conclusions Handgrip strength, unlike self-reported PA, was associated with brain structure and cognitive performance, highlighting the importance of PA assessment modality in brain health research. Mediation of associations between handgrip strength and cognition by PSMD suggest white matter microstructural injury as one pathway linking neuromuscular and cognitive function. Clinical Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT03934957.

item.title: Metformin Preserves Regional Brain Glucose Uptake, Structure, and Functional Connectivity in Adults with Insulin Resistance.
item.description:
The Journal of clinical investigation
Background Dementia is a rapidly expanding public health problem with major socio-economic burden. Insulin resistance (IR) is a prevalent but modifiable risk factor for dementia, yet its effects on brain structure, functional connectivity, and metabolism remain incompletely understood. Methods Regional brain glucose uptake (PET), volumes (MRI), functional connectivity (fMRI), and cognition (NIH Toolbox) was measured in 72 adults with or without markers of IR. To evaluate reversibility of IR-associated brain deficits, forty older adults with IR were randomized to forty weeks of metformin or placebo, and brain measures were repeated. As a proof-of-concept experiment, we developed a conditional brain-specific insulin receptor knockout mouse and assessed brain mitochondrial function and cognition. Results In older adults with markers of IR is associated with diminished total and regional brain volumes in areas critical for neuronal connectivity, memory, and learning, including cerebral white matter and the hippocampus. Reduced functional connectivity between brain regions detrimental for cognition was also noted. Further, we demonstrated that ATP production, essential for neuronal connectivity, was diminished in neuron-specific insulin receptor knockout mice accompanied by deficits in hippocampal- and prefrontal-dependent tasks. Forty weeks of metformin improved systemic insulin sensitivity concurrent to preserved brain glucose uptake, volume, and functional connectivity within specific regions central to decision-making and learning. Metformin was also associated with an improved composite measure of processing speed and working memory. Conclusion These findings highlight IR as a key regulator of brain metabolism and support the concept that insulin sensitization can prevent neurobiological deficits in older people with IR.

item.title: Substantial evidence against sex differences in bed nucleus of the stria terminalis volume in the human brain.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
"The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST) is a sexually dimorphic basal forebrain region" is a claim prevalent across rodent and human neuroscience research, arising from the observation that it is substantially larger in male versus female brains. Despite the pervasiveness of this claim, which may have implications for understanding sex differences in anxiety and substance use disorders, inspection of the literature reveals a complex and nuanced picture. Research on volumetric human BNST sex differences comes from a handful of mostly small-scale post-mortem studies and two MRI studies, between them reporting no, moderate, or very large differences. This indicates the need for a more detailed systematic investigation. Addressing this, we developed a novel 3T T1-weighted (T1w) manual segmentation protocol for the BNST, which was applied to sub-millimetre resolution T1w structural MRI data in 170 young human adults. Using a Bayesian modelling approach, taking into account existing data and accounting for total brain volume, age, and sibship, we find substantial evidence favouring no sex difference in total BNST volume. We recommend that researchers exercise caution when reporting evidence of BNST sexual dimorphism, particularly when translating findings from rodent models in which the BNST may play a different, olfaction-focused, role.

item.title: Longitudinal quantitative streamline tractography: Robust estimation of white matter connectivity differences.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Longitudinal probing of structural connectivity via diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is experiencing uptake. However, the detection of biological effects is significantly hampered by the limitations of cross-sectional streamline tractography, where even small changes in the dMRI signal can produce drastically different trajectories and, therefore, quantitative parameterisation; if not properly dealt with, such effects will manifest as spurious longitudinal change, which can obscure subtle biological differences. To address this challenge, we here introduce a novel quantitative streamline tractography framework tailored for longitudinal analysis, wherein an individual's streamline trajectories remain fixed throughout the analysis, allowing only their ascribed density weights to vary between sessions. We present two strategies by which these quantitative streamline weights can be determined, both extensions of the widely adopted SIFT2 method. The performance of this framework is benchmarked against cross-sectional reconstruction with and without SIFT2 optimisation, in both in silico dMRI phantoms with known ground truths and three distinct human in vivo cohorts with clear a priori expectations of biological effects. We demonstrate that the proposed framework drastically reduces methodological imprecisions in synthetic dMRI phantoms and enhances statistical sensitivity and specificity to biological effects in human cohorts, enabling more robust quantification of longitudinal structural connectivity differences.

item.title: Annual Research Review: A probe into sensitive periods - how the developmental timing of adverse childhood experiences influences brain structure and function - a systematic review.
item.description:
Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
It is proposed that adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) - potent predictors of mental illness - exert time-dependent effects on neurodevelopment, reflecting periods of heightened neuroplasticity and developmental sensitivity. We systematically reviewed neuroimaging studies examining the role of timing in the association of ACE exposure with brain structure and function across the lifespan. Across 43 studies spanning childhood to adulthood, findings most consistently implicate earlier onset and longer duration of adversity in alterations to limbic and paralimbic regions, including the hippocampus, amygdala, cerebellum and global brain measures. However, evidence for discrete sensitive periods is mixed and varies by brain system, outcome and analytic approach, with no consistent pattern of sensitive periods emerging across adversity types and functional neuroimaging studies remaining comparatively limited. Progress in the field is further constrained by substantial conceptual and methodological heterogeneity, including inconsistent operationalisation of sensitive periods, reliance on retrospective ACE measures and predominantly cross-sectional designs. Moving forward, we argue that advancing the field will require reconceptualising sensitive periods as probabilistic, system-specific and shaped by the nature, timing and chronicity of adversity, rather than as fixed developmental windows. Integrating longitudinal assessment of adversity and neurodevelopment with measures of the neurobiological processes underlying plasticity may help determine whether sensitive periods are better characterised by underlying neuroplasticity than chronological age alone. Improved understanding of these developmental processes may ultimately help inform the timing and targeting of preventive and therapeutic interventions for young people exposed to adversity.
